And if nobody can secure the dog, exception it. No package is worth a bite.
Remember: stand still, never run. And if nobody can secure the dog, exception it. No package is worth a bite.
Heat
Morning. Heat advisory today. Coolers are stocked, take extra water.
What is the first sign you should act on?
Headache, dizziness, cramps or feeling sick. Stop, cool down, drink and call in.
Act at the first symptom. Heat exhaustion turns into heat stroke fast.
When I stop sweating. That is the real warning.
Hot dry skin is a late sign of heat stroke, which is a medical emergency. Act long before that.
Act on early heat symptoms: headache, dizziness, cramps, nausea.
When I feel thirsty.
Thirst means you are already behind on fluids. Drink on a schedule in this weather.
Drink before you are thirsty and use the AC between stops.
Act at the first headache or dizziness, not later. Drink before you are thirsty and use the AC between stops.
Winter driving
Morning. Overnight freeze, so walkways and steps will be sheet ice in the shade.
How are you handling the ice today?
Short steps, feet flat, hold the handrail, slow down, and double my following distance in the truck.
Slow and flat-footed. Most winter injuries are in the first three steps off the truck.
Normal pace. I will just be careful on the worst bits.
Black ice does not announce itself. Treat every surface as slick until proven otherwise.
On ice, slow everything down: walking and driving.
Good. Take the time you need.
Slow it all down today, walking and driving. Take the time you need.
Scanning and exceptions
Morning. Customer service flagged a few stops last week that were marked delivered with no proof.
When does a package get scanned?
Morning briefing check
Before it leaves the truck, so I catch wrong-stop pieces and see signature requirements.
Scan first. It catches misloads before you have walked to the door.
At the door, right before I hand it over.
Better than nothing, but you have already walked. Scan at the truck.
At the end of the street, in a batch.
Batch scanning hides misdeliveries and breaks the tracking customers rely on.
Scan each package before it leaves the truck.
And if it cannot be delivered, code it properly and leave a door tag.
Scan every piece at the truck. And if it cannot be delivered, code it properly and leave a door tag.
During the pre-trip, the brake pedal slowly sinks while you hold steady pressure. What do you do?
Pump it a few times, then drive carefully to the first stop
Flag it: the van stays put until it is fixed
Note it on the report and check it again at lunch
Drive on unless the brake warning light comes on
A pedal that creeps down under steady pressure is a brake fault. It is flagged and fixed before the van moves.
What does a full stop at a stop sign mean?
Slowing to walking pace right at the line
Wheels stopped behind the line, then look
Stopping fully only when cross traffic is coming
Stopping anywhere before you enter the junction
The wheels stop behind the line for a moment, then you look both ways. Rolling stops are the classic delivery-driver citation.
Turning right in a step van, the rear wheels…
Follow the exact path the front wheels took
Cut inside the front wheels, toward the curb
Swing wide, out into the next lane over
Only matter when you are reversing
The rear wheels cut inside the front ones. Swing wider and slower so they stay off the curb and the sidewalk.
You have to back up to reach a loading door. What comes first?
Hazard lights on, then back up slowly
Get out and look at what is behind you
Check both mirrors: getting out wastes time
Sound the horn twice, then back up slowly
Back as little as possible, and when you must: get out and look first, then back slowly using your mirrors.
A ball rolls into the street ahead. What should you expect?
Nothing more: the ball itself is the hazard
A child may follow it, so slow down and cover the brake
The car behind you to brake hard for it
To steer around it without slowing down
A ball in the road often means a child is about to follow it. Slow down and be ready to stop.
Before lifting a heavy box from the floor, you should…
Bend at the waist and lift it in one quick move
Step in close, bend your knees, back straight
Twist your body to carry it out to the side
Lift it at arm's length so it stays clean
Get close to the load, bend the knees, keep your back straight and the load against your body. Let your legs do the work.
A package is too heavy or awkward to lift safely alone. What now?
Drag it across the floor to where it goes
Use a hand truck or get a second person
Lift it in two quick jerks to save your back
Leave it on the floor for the next shift
Use the equipment (hand truck, dolly) or a team lift. Your back has a long career ahead of it.
Why turn a package to check every side before you place it?
To find the heaviest end so you can lift it right
A handling mark may be on a side you missed
To check that the tape is holding on every seam
You only need to for international packages
Handling marks (this way up, fragile, hazard diamonds) can be on any side. Read all six.
A box on the belt is leaking an unknown liquid. You should…
Wipe it dry and send it on down the belt
Hands off: step back, isolate it and report it
Open it carefully to see what is leaking
Put it at the bottom so it can't drip on others
Leaking or damaged: don't touch the contents. Isolate the package and report it.
When sorting, the package label and the bin disagree. What do you trust?
The bin you usually use for that street
The label: read it and route it there
Whichever is faster at that moment
Neither: ask the customer about it later
Read the label every time. A misroute costs far more time later than the second it takes to read.
An angry customer says their package is late. The best first step is…
Explain that the delay wasn't your fault
Acknowledge it, then say what you can do
Give them the depot number and move on
Promise them it will arrive later today
A calm voice and acknowledging the problem de-escalate. Then offer what you actually can do. Don't promise what you can't.
At a business, a receptionist signs for a package addressed to a colleague. Whose name do you record?
The addressee's, since it is their package
The receptionist's, as they printed it
The company's name from the label
Nobody's: the scan alone is enough
Record the printed name of whoever actually signed, even when it isn't the addressee.
A signature-required package, and nobody answers the door. You…
Leave it somewhere hidden and take a photo
Record an exception and leave a door tag
Sign for it yourself so the customer gets it
Leave it with the neighbor next door
A signature-required package is never left unattended. Record the exception, leave a door tag and keep the package.
A customer wants to chat and you are behind schedule. You should…
Cut them off and walk back to the van
Stay friendly, then close it politely
Explain how many stops you still have left
Keep working and ignore them until they stop
Stay friendly and warm but brief. Different customers need different styles; all of them deserve courtesy.
A customer is aggressive and you feel unsafe. What do you do?
Stand your ground and argue your side firmly
Get to safety, don't engage, and report it
Finish the delivery quickly, whatever happens
Calm them down by giving them the package
Your safety comes first. Leave, don't escalate, and report it to your manager.
The label says Maple Court, but you are on Maple Avenue, where the number doesn't exist. You…
Deliver to the closest number on the avenue
Check the address, then ask dispatch instead of guessing
